query: Equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its quaternary and ternary subsets provide 16 candidate alloys, nine of which are single-phase FCC after thermomechanical processing. Early reports associated increasing constituent count with greater strength, but that simple relationship is no longer generally accepted. Despite extensive experimental and theoretical investigation, the origins of differences in deformation and failure behavior remain unresolved; practical interpretation must also account for constituent cost and overall cost-performance balance. What testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs these mechanical-property differences and why? Define a controlled investigation, the observations predicted relative to the equiatomic quinary baseline, the limits within which the hypothesis should apply, the prior evidence supporting it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Mechanical-property differences in these single‐phase FCC high‐entropy alloys arise because variations in local atomic-scale lattice distortions and short-range chemical ordering—caused by subtle changes in the elemental mix—modulate dislocation mobility during deformation.
generation.material_initial_state: All alloys (equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni baseline and its quaternary and ternary subsets) are processed to yield a single-phase FCC microstructure via consistent thermomechanical processing (e.g., homogenization at high temperature, controlled quenching, and subsequent deformation to refine the microstructure).
generation.intervention: Alter the alloy composition by selectively removing or substituting one or more elements from the equiatomic five-element baseline to create quaternary and ternary variants, thus provoking variations in local lattice distortions and chemical short-range order while maintaining the FCC phase.
generation.conditions: Mechanical tensile tests conducted at room temperature using a controlled strain rate (e.g., ~10^(-3) s^(-1)) together with detailed microstructural analysis (TEM, high-resolution STEM, and atom probe tomography) to characterize local lattice distortions and chemical ordering. The processing and testing conditions are kept identical across compositions.
generation.structural_mediator: Local lattice distortions and short-range chemical order established by atomic size mismatches and solute-solute interactions.
generation.mechanism: Variations in elemental composition cause differences in atomic size mismatch and bonding environments, which in turn generate distinct degrees of local lattice distortion and short-range order. These structural features modulate dislocation nucleation and glide—altering yield strength and work hardening—by either impeding or facilitating dislocation motion during deformation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni baseline, alloys that experience increased lattice distortions (due to, for example, a higher mismatch from removal or substitution of a particular element) are expected to exhibit higher yield strengths and modified work-hardening rates, whereas alloys with lower distortions might demonstrate lower strength. The hypothesis predicts a correlation between the magnitude of local distortion/chemical ordering and the observed mechanical properties, within the range applicable to single-phase FCC microstructures.
generation.baseline: Equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni high-entropy alloy processed to be a single-phase FCC structure under identical thermomechanical conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies only to single-phase FCC alloys with controlled microstructures (uniform grain size and absence of secondary phases). It does not extend to cases where precipitation or transformation effects predominate, or when processing introduces considerable microstructural heterogeneities.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative correlations between measured lattice distortions and the magnitude of strength enhancement are uncertain, and the interplay with other strengthening mechanisms (e.g., traditional solution hardening) may complicate the attribution solely to local distortions and short-range order.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare samples of the baseline equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy and carefully selected quaternary/ternary variants using the same thermomechanical processing route. Perform room temperature tensile tests at a fixed strain rate while concurrently quantifying local lattice distortions and chemical order (via high-resolution TEM/STEM and atom probe tomography). The key is to correlate measured local distortion metrics with yield strength and work-hardening behavior.
measurements: Local lattice distortion magnitude (e.g., via diffraction or STEM imaging)
Chemical short-range ordering metrics (via atom probe tomography)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If alloys predicted to have higher local distortions do not exhibit correspondingly higher yield strengths and altered work-hardening rates relative to the equiatomic baseline, or if variations in mechanical properties occur without measurable differences in local lattice distortions and chemical ordering, then the hypothesis is falsified.
